standard.title: Different Experiences and Perspectives of Colonisers and Asian Peoples
standard.description: different experiences and perspectives of colonisers and Asian peoples and the impact of these on changes to society, ideas, beliefs and values in an Asian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the features of the selected Asian society (K19), the causes and effects of European contact (K20), key events and figures (K21), and continuities and changes around 1900 (K22). This descriptor asks them to move from description and analysis of events to explicit perspective-taking and historiographical reflection — examining how the same colonial encounter was experienced and interpreted differently by colonisers and colonised peoples, and how those interpretations have themselves changed over time.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate different experiences and perspectives of colonisers and Asian peoples and explain the impact of these on changes to society, ideas, beliefs and values.

nodes.label: Comparing perspectives on European colonisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare and contrast different perspectives about the effect of European colonisation on the selected Asian society, drawing on sources from both coloniser and colonised viewpoints.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and compare at least two different perspectives on European colonisation of the selected Asian society — one from the coloniser side and one from the colonised side.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and contrast different perspectives about the effect of European colonisation on Asian countries — examining how colonisers framed their presence (commercial benefit, civilising mission, strategic necessity) versus how colonised peoples experienced and articulated their situation (exploitation, loss of sovereignty, cultural threat); examine how the same events (e.g. the Boxer Rebellion, the Sepoy Uprising, the Java War) were narrated differently depending on perspective.
wider: Examine how internal divisions within colonised societies shaped responses to colonialism — investigating groups within the selected Asian society who cooperated with colonial authorities versus those who resisted, and analysing why people in the same society responded differently

Investigate how the experiences of women within both coloniser and colonised communities shaped their relationship to colonial change — examining gendered perspectives that differ from male-centred historical narratives

Analyse a specific colonial event from a minimum of three perspectives — e.g. the Boxer Rebellion from the perspective of Qing officials, foreign missionaries, and ordinary Chinese participants — to examine the multiplicity of viewpoints within a single society

response_modes.reason: The coloniser/colonised binary, while useful, risks oversimplifying — widening to include perspectives within each side (reformers vs traditionalists; collaborators vs resistors) gives a more accurate historical picture.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The perspective analysis enabled by this descriptor is one of the most powerful historical thinking moves in the curriculum — it requires students to step outside a single narrative and examine how position, experience, and interest shape what people see and say. This connects directly to the historical skills strand.
success_criteria: Compares at least two distinct perspectives on European colonisation of the selected Asian society, identifying specific differences in how the situation was experienced or framed
Explains at least one way these different perspectives impacted on changes to society, ideas, beliefs or values

nodes.label: Historical interpretations — how historians have viewed colonial influence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare similarities and differences in historians' views about the significance of Western colonial influences on the selected Asian society, recognising that historical interpretation is shaped by perspective and context.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different historical interpretations of Western colonial influence on the selected Asian society and explain how they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Compare similarities and differences in historians' views about the significance of Western colonial influences — including: colonial-era accounts that emphasised 'civilising' benefits; nationalist historiography that emphasised exploitation and resistance; post-colonial historiography that examined structural power and long-term consequences; contemporary scholarship that seeks to recover colonised people's own voices and perspectives. Explain how historians' own positions and contexts have shaped their interpretations.
wider: Examine how the historiography of colonialism in the selected Asian society has changed since decolonisation — investigating how scholars from the formerly colonised nation have reframed the historical narrative

Investigate a specific contested historical question about the selected Asian society (e.g. was British rule beneficial or detrimental to India? Was the Meiji Restoration a genuine modernisation or a defensive response to coercion?) and assess the evidence each side uses

Examine how the history of European colonialism in Asia is taught in different national contexts today — and assess how national education systems continue to shape the interpretive frameworks students encounter

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the perspective analysis (Node 1) with historiographical awareness — moving students from primary source perspectives to secondary source interpretation. It is the most sophisticated analytical move in the Asian history depth study.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two different historians' views about Western colonial influence on the selected society and explains how they differ
Explains at least one factor (historian's context, methodology, or sources used) that contributed to different historical interpretations
